hints: Focus on how dehydration works, the OH group leaves together with an H from a neighbouring carbon to form a C=C double bond.
Check each alcohol for how many different neighbouring carbons with H atoms are next to the C-OH carbon.
Look for the alcohol where removing H from two different sides gives a double bond in two different positions, making two positional isomers.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for dehydration**

Think of dehydration as removing water. The OH leaves from one carbon and an H leaves from an adjacent carbon.

$$\text{alcohol} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4, \text{ heat}} \text{alkene} + H_2O$$

**Identify each alcohol**

Name them calmly from the displayed formulae. A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (butan-1-ol). B is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (butan-2-ol). C is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$ (2-methylpropan-1-ol). D is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COH}$ (2-methylpropan-2-ol).

**Count the different elimination routes**

For two different alkene products, the C-OH carbon must have two non-equivalent adjacent carbons that both carry H. In B, the OH is on C2, with $\text{CH}_3$ on the left (C1) and $\text{CH}_2$ on the right (C3). Removing H from C1 gives $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (but-1-ene). Removing H from C3 gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ (but-2-ene).

**Confirm structural isomerism**

But-1-ene and but-2-ene have the same molecular formula, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, but the double bond is in a different position. They are positional structural isomers, so this alcohol meets the requirement.

options.A: Butan-1-ol has OH on C1. H can only be removed from the one adjacent carbon, C2, to give $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (but-1-ene) only. There is no second route, so only one alkene forms.
options.B: Butan-2-ol has OH on the middle carbon C2. Elimination of H from C1 gives but-1-ene and elimination of H from C3 gives but-2-ene. Both are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ but with the C=C in different places, so they are structural (positional) isomers.
options.C: 2-methylpropan-1-ol has OH on C1. The only adjacent carbon is C2, so loss of H can only give $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=CH}_2$ (2-methylpropene). Only one alkene product is possible.
options.D: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary with OH on a carbon with no H. All three adjacent methyl groups are identical, so removing H from any of them gives the same product, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=CH}_2$ (2-methylpropene). Only one distinct alkene forms.
